name: Ali ibn Abi Talib
info: Ali ibn Abi Talib was the cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, the fourth Rashidun caliph from 656 to 661 and, for Shia Muslims, the first Imam and rightful successor to the Prophet.

facts.born: c. 600 in Mecca, son of Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Fatima bint Asad, of the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh
facts.died: c. 28 January 661 (19 Ramadan 40 AH) at the Great Mosque of Kufa, struck during the morning prayer by the Kharijite Ibn Muljam; other given dates are 26 and 30 January, and he died of his wounds about two days later
facts.role: Fourth Rashidun caliph, 656 to 661; for Sunni Muslims the last of the rightly guided caliphs, for Shia Muslims the first Imam and the designated successor of Muhammad
facts.known: early support of Muhammad; marriage to Fatima; Ghadir Khumm; the Battle of the Camel; the Battle of Siffin; the Kharijites; Nahj al-balagha

t: Raised in Muhammad's household, Ali was among the first to accept Islam, married Muhammad's daughter Fatima and served as his secretary, deputy and standard-bearer in Medina.
After Muhammad's death in 632 Sunni and Shia Muslims tell the succession differently: Sunnis accept Abu Bakr's appointment, while Shia Muslims hold that Muhammad had designated Ali at Ghadir Khumm.

Ali became caliph in 656 after Uthman's assassination, fought civil wars against Aisha, Talha, Zubayr and Mu'awiya, and was murdered in Kufa in 661, after which Mu'awiya founded the Umayyad Caliphate.
dyk: Ali's own father, Abu Talib, raised Muhammad, and Ali later came under Muhammad's guardianship when he was about five years old.
ev: Ali is born in Mecca to Abu Talib and Fatima bint Asad
He stays in Muhammad's bed as a decoy on the night Muhammad leaves for Medina
At Ghadir Khumm Muhammad says, "He whose mawla I am, Ali is his mawla"
The electoral council chooses Uthman over Ali
Ali takes the oath as caliph and wins the Battle of the Camel
The Battle of Siffin against Mu'awiya ends in a call for arbitration
He defeats the Kharijites at the Battle of Nahrawan and loses Egypt
He is assassinated at Kufa and Mu'awiya later founds the Umayyad Caliphate

sections.early:
Ali was born around 600 in Mecca to Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Fatima bint Asad, in the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh. Tradition says that he may have been born inside the Ka'ba and, possibly, on 13 Rajab, the date Shia Muslims celebrate each year. His father had raised Muhammad after Muhammad's parents died, and when Abu Talib fell into poverty Ali came under the guardianship of Muhammad and his wife Khadija at about the age of five.

At about eleven Ali was among the first to accept Muhammad's teachings. Sunni and Shia scholars debate whether he did so after Khadija or after Khadija and Abu Bakr, though the earliest sources place him before Abu Bakr. According to the Sunni historian al-Tabari (d. 923), about three years after the first revelation Muhammad gathered his relatives for a feast and asked for their help; Ali, then about fourteen, was the only one to offer it, and Muhammad told the guests that Ali was his brother and successor. The Shia interpretation is that Muhammad had thereby already designated Ali as his successor. During the Meccan years Ali supported the small community, especially the poor.
sections.rise:
In 622, when Muhammad learned of a plot against his life, Ali stayed behind in Muhammad's bed as a decoy, and later returned the goods that had been entrusted to Muhammad. A Quranic passage about a man who gives his life away to please God is said to refer to this. In Medina, Muhammad chose Ali as his brother when pairing Muslims in fraternity pacts, and around 623 to 625 gave him his daughter Fatima in marriage. Muhammad had earlier turned down proposals for Fatima from Abu Bakr and Umar.

In Medina Ali acted as Muhammad's secretary and deputy and was one of the scribes who wrote down the Quran. In 628 he wrote the terms of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiya. In 631 Muhammad sent him to preach Islam in Yemen, where the Hamdanids converted peacefully. He accompanied Muhammad on every campaign but Tabuk, where he was left in charge of Medina, and Muhammad is reported to have asked him there, "Are you not content, Ali, to stand to me as Aaron stood to Moses, except that there will be no prophet after me?" For the Shia this hadith signifies his right to succeed Muhammad. He was standard-bearer at Badr and Khaybar, and defended Muhammad at Uhud and Hunayn.
sections.deeds:
Returning from the pilgrimage in 632, Muhammad halted the pilgrims at Ghadir Khumm, took Ali by the hand and said, "He whose mawla I am, Ali is his mawla." The authenticity of the event is rarely contested, but the meaning of mawla is disputed along sectarian lines. Shia sources read it as leader, master and patron, and so as the investiture of Ali with Muhammad's religious and political authority; Sunni sources read it as love or support for Ali, or as a statement about their friendship, and see it as a reply to earlier complaints about him.

After 656 Ali dismissed nearly all of Uthman's governors, whom he considered corrupt, and shared the treasury funds equally among Muslims, as Muhammad had. Some who lost by this soon revolted, among them Mu'awiya, the governor of Syria. Ali forbade his soldiers to loot, pardoned his enemies in victory and prevented the enslavement of women, and practices of this kind were later enshrined in Islamic law. He regarded himself as the community's religious authority as well as its temporal leader, and some of his supporters felt a bond of spiritual loyalty (walaya) to him. He made Kufa in Iraq his base. Some have criticised him for political naivety and rigidity; others have praised him for righteousness.
sections.opponents:
When Muhammad died in 632, a group of Muslims met at the Saqifa in Ali's absence and appointed Abu Bakr. Ali's supporters, including Zubayr and Abbas, gathered in protest at his house. Al-Tabari reports that Umar led an armed mob there and threatened to burn the house unless they pledged to Abu Bakr; Shia sources attribute Fatima's death and miscarriage to an attack on her house, which Sunnis categorically reject. Ali most likely pledged to Abu Bakr only after Fatima died within six months of her father. Sunni sources minimise the conflicts between Ali and the first caliphs, while those conflicts are probably magnified in Shia sources.

As caliph, Ali was opposed first by Aisha, Talha and Zubayr, who broke their oaths and demanded punishment for Uthman's killers; Ali defeated them in December 656 at the Battle of the Camel. He then fought Mu'awiya, who demanded revenge for Uthman, at Siffin in the summer of 657. The fighting stopped when Syrians raised pages of the Quran on lances, and Ali, under pressure from his own army, accepted arbitration, most likely against his own judgement. The arbitration split his camp. The Kharijites, who left under the slogan "No judgment but that of God", were crushed at Nahrawan in 658; some have criticised Ali for killing them, others hold it was necessary. The Ibadis hold that he forfeited his right to lead by accepting arbitration.
sections.last:
After Nahrawan, Ali could not raise enough support for a second campaign against Syria, perhaps because his soldiers were demoralised or because tribal leaders had been swayed by Mu'awiya. He lost Egypt in 658, and Mu'awiya sent raiding parties against the Euphrates, the Hejaz and Yemen. A new offensive was planned for late winter 661. On 28 January 661, or 26 or 30 January by other accounts, the Kharijite Ibn Muljam struck him on the head with a poison-coated sword during the morning prayer at the Great Mosque of Kufa, in revenge for Nahrawan. Ali died about two days later, aged sixty-two or sixty-three.

Fearing that his body might be dug up and profaned, his followers kept the burial place secret, and it remains uncertain. Najaf, identified in the time of Harun al-Rashid, is the main shrine and a major Shia pilgrimage site; other sites claimed include Mazar, Baghdad, Damascus, Medina and Ray. His son Hasan was acknowledged as caliph in Kufa but abdicated in August 661 to Mu'awiya, who founded the Umayyad Caliphate, persecuted Ali's family and supporters and authorised the cursing of Ali in communal prayers.
sections.legacy:
Sunni Muslims regard Ali as the fourth and last of the rashidun, or rightly guided, caliphs, a close companion of Muhammad and an authority on the Quran and Islamic law. Shia Muslims venerate him as the first Imam and the rightful successor to Muhammad by divine designation, and the word shi'a itself is short for the followers of Ali. The Twelvers trace the line of imams through Hasan and Husayn, who was killed at Karbala in 680, to the twelfth, who they hold remains in occultation. Nearly all Sufi orders trace their lineage to Muhammad through Ali; the Ibadis hold he lost his right to lead at Siffin. Some groups such as the Alawites attribute divinity to him, a view that most Shia reject.

The most famous collection attributed to him is Nahj al-balagha, compiled in the 11th century by Sharif al-Radi, with sermons, letters and sayings, including a letter of instructions to al-Ashtar; recent academic research has attributed most of it to Ali, though its authenticity has long been debated. Historians note that accounts of Ali are often tendentious and were written down centuries later, and the scholars Caetani and Madelung differ over how to treat partisan reports.

summary: Ali ibn Abi Talib (c. 600 to 661) was Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law and the fourth Rashidun caliph from 656. Sunni Muslims honour him as a rightly guided caliph and Shia Muslims as the first Imam and rightful successor. He was assassinated at Kufa.
